sources.title: Mohammed Hassen, The Oromo of Ethiopia, 1500 to 1850: with special emphasis on the Gibe region (1983)
sources.note: Original SOAS doctoral research. Full repository abstract checked through indexed text; direct repository and thesis PDF access failed. Uses abstract-level findings on sixteenth-century migration, Gibe state formation, Islamic learning and organized trade; no claim to have read the full thesis.

sources.title: UNESCO, Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo (2016 inscription)
sources.note: Official nomination summary checked through full indexed text. Five classes, rotating eight-year leadership, male membership, consultation of women, oral historians, sycamore meeting spaces, home and school transmission. Describes a living institution, not uniform practice at every historical date.

sources.title: Oromo community consent for the Gada UNESCO nomination (2015 submission)
sources.note: Original bilingual English/Oromo community consent packet. Direct PDF access challenged; exact indexed text checked with query site:ich.unesco.org/doc/src/30581 "Sirna Gadaa Oromoo". Signature table, rows 61 to 70, headings Umurii (Age), Mallattoo (signature). Does not quote personal applicants. Contemporary writing only.

sources.title: Donald L. Coppock, The Borana Plateau of Southern Ethiopia: synthesis of pastoral research, development and change, 1980 to 1991 (1994)
sources.note: ILCA original research synthesis, full HTML directly read. Chapter 4 sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.5; Chapter 2 section 2.4.1.7 directly read at https://www.fao.org/4/x5461e/x5461e0c.htm. All chapters treated as one work for word budget. Dated field observations, not asserted as sixteenth-century customs.

sources.title: Waktole Tiki, Gufu Oba and Terje Tvedt, Human stewardship or ruining cultural landscapes of the ancient Tula wells, southern Ethiopia (2011)
sources.note: Original research, Geographical Journal 177, pp. 62 to 78. Full publisher abstract indexed and read: five of nine well clusters, operation for more than five centuries and community perceptions of changing land use. Does not resolve the identity of the first builders.

sources.title: Hiroki Ishikawa, Migration to the Christian Kingdom of Northern Ethiopia and Its Consequences (2008)
sources.note: Original historical study, Journal of African Studies 72, pp. 1 to 15. Publisher abstract directly read. Distinguishes migrant groups including formerly subordinate communities from the Oromo with whom they later cooperated. Only the stated conclusion about regional long-distance trade is used.

sources.title: South African History Online, Eastern Cape Wars of Dispossession, 1779 to 1878
sources.note: Institutional historical account directly checked in indexed text, particularly final-war section. Broad chronology only; dated colonial terminology and sweeping claims of total cultural destruction are not adopted.

sources.title: Timothy J. Stapleton, A Military History of South Africa (2010)
sources.note: Original scholarly synthesis. Full PDF directly read, chapter The Cape-Xhosa War of 1877 to 1878, printed pp. 56 to 62 (human PDF pp. 70 to 76). Selected passages on dispossession, divided alliances and Sandile’s death.

sources.title: J. B. Peires, The Central Beliefs of the Xhosa Cattle-Killing (1987)
sources.note: Original historical research, Journal of African History 28(1), pp. 43 to 63. Publisher extract directly checked in indexed text; direct article page rate-limited. Extract supports 1854 lungsickness and the fusion of indigenous and Christian ideas. Full-paper access is not claimed.

sources.title: Lindsay Hooper, Some Nguni Crafts, Part 3: Wood-Carving (1981)
sources.note: South African Museum original object and documentary study, Annals 70(3). Full PDF directly read. Only explicitly Xhosa subsections used, not adjacent Zulu or Mpondo descriptions. Printed pp. 166, 182 and 183, especially necklace SAM-10920 and Figure 16.

sources.title: Don Duco, Tobacco pipes from the Xhosa, from traditional utensil to souvenir item (2013)
sources.note: Amsterdam Pipe Museum original collection study; full English article directly read at this language-route URL. Only material analysis and production process used. Its outdated broad political and cultural introduction is not relied upon.

sources.title: Jeff Opland, The First Novel in Xhosa (2007)
sources.note: Original literary research, Research in African Literatures 38(4), pp. 87 to 110. Full indexed passages checked; direct PDF denied. Exact Indaba (News), dates 1862 to 1865, named contributors and Uhambo lomhambi (1867); later Gqoba editorial and educational criticism. Earlier repository address https://eprints.soas.ac.uk/7609/1/first_novel.pdf indexes the same work; treated as one source.

sources.title: Nelson Mandela, original autobiographical manuscript: Childhood Days
sources.note: Primary memoir preserved by the Nelson Mandela Foundation; full PDF directly read, chapter 1, typed p. 13. Later Thembu childhood is explicitly contextual, not a description of all historical Xhosa or an identification of the two political communities.

sources.title: Robert Mantran, Karamanlı, TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi (2001)
sources.note: Scholarly encyclopedia by an Ottoman historian, with Ottoman archive citations; full Turkish article directly read. Political dates 1711, 1793 to 1795 interruption, 1832 crisis and Ottoman landing 27 May 1835. No inference that regional identity ended with the dynasty.

sources.title: LaVerle Berry, Historical Setting, in Helen Chapin Metz, Libya: A Country Study (1989)
sources.note: Library of Congress Federal Research Division. Public PDF downloaded into cache and directly read with pdfplumber, printed pp. 18 to 24 (human PDF pp. 50 to 56). Public text avoids dated cultural stereotypes in the original.

sources.title: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, Barbary Wars, 1801 to 1805 and 1815 to 1816
sources.note: Official diplomatic-history article, full HTML directly read. Uses only Tripoli’s 1801 to 1805 war and treaty. Does not transfer Algiers-specific events to Tripoli.

sources.title: Mohamed Mustafa Khazmi and Abd. Rahman Bin Hj. Hamzah, Secrets of the Foundational Paintings of the Karamanli Era Mosques in the Old City of Tripoli (2022)
sources.note: Original field photographs and transcription, pp. 738 to 755. PDF directly read; downloaded and rendered human PDF pp. 6 and 7 (printed 743 and 744). Figure 5 photograph and Figure 6 transcription visually confirm opening بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. Public sample normalizes diacritics. Only observed architectural features and inscription used; poorly translated measurements, generalized aesthetic claims and disputed Gurgi construction dates are excluded.

sources.title: Ahmed Saadaoui and Ali Cheib Ben Sassi, La mosquée Gurgi à Tripoli et son waqf, Al-Sabîl 17 (2024)
sources.note: Original archival and architectural research. Full trilingual abstract directly read; linked article download fails. Journal labels issue 17, 2024 although webpage URL dates 2026. Only abstract-level claims used: Mustafa Gurgi’s patronage, relation to Ahmad Pasha mosque and 1844 waqf document. No exact construction date used because this study and 2022 article disagree.

sources.title: Miss Tully, Narrative of a Ten Years’ Residence at Tripoli in Africa (1816)
sources.note: Original letters from the British consular household; author conventionally called Miss Tully. Public-domain Wellcome copy, OCR downloaded directly from https://archive.org/download/b22013647/b22013647_djvu.txt and checked. Letters 9 September 1783, printed pp. 24 to 26; 27 May 1785, pp. 83 to 84. Foreign elite observer, explicitly attributed; racist generalizations, medical theories and blanket claims of uniform housing excluded. All five passages counted together.

proposedOverrides.summary: Tripolitania linked western Libya to Mediterranean and Saharan networks.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Broad ethnolinguistic record, not one centralized empire. Imported 1530 to 1815 snapshots lie mainly in southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya; narrative explicitly distinguishes Gibe kingdoms and later Borana field observations. No aliases, invented founding date, or single conquest endpoint.

Imported 1783 to 1878 Eastern Cape outline is a broad Xhosa label, not proof of one uniform kingdom. Gcaleka and Rharhabe are distinguished; Mfengu alliances acknowledged. Thembu childhood is expressly later, related linguistic context, not an alias. No shared cards.

Imported 1715 to 1878 polygon [12.116,30.222,18.884,32.879] represents western coastal Libya, not the whole Ottoman province that sometimes shared its name. Separate from Cyrenaica. Dynasty 1711 to 1835, with 1793 to 1795 interruption, and direct Ottoman phase distinguished. No false fall in 1878.
